Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)
- coderabbit:code-reviewer: Specialized CodeRabbit code review agent that performs thorough analysis of code changes (Tools: All tools)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- feature-factory:spec-challenger: Adversarial reviewer for a feature spec / design document. Use after a spec is drafted (Stage 2 of the feature-factory pipeline) to attack it before any code is written - finding gaps, ambiguities, unstated assumptions, edge cases, and weak design decisions. Returns a severity-tagged critique and an overall verdict. This is the automated replacement for "ask another Opus to challenge the spec". (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

## plugin:bio-research:biorxiv
An MCP server for accessing bioRxiv and medRxiv preprint servers.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search preprints, get preprint details, list subject categories
- Prompts: Analyze preprint methodology and findings

bioRxiv is a preprint server for biological sciences operated by Cold Spring
Harbor Laboratory. It hosts research manuscripts that have NOT undergone peer
review. This server wraps the official bioRxiv API to provide structured access
to preprint metadata, abstracts, and full-text PDFs.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_preprints: Find preprints by date range and/or subject category (no keyword, author, or full-text search) - primary discovery tool
• get_preprint: Get full details for a specific preprint by DOI
• get_categories: List available subject categories for filtering
• search_published_preprints: Find preprints that have been formally published in journals
• funder_search: Find preprints by funding source (NIH, etc.)
• get_statistics: Usage and submission statistics

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive literature analysis:
1. Use search_preprints to find relevant preprints by date range and category
2. Use get_preprint for detailed information on promising results
3. Use search_published_preprints to check if preprints have been peer-reviewed and published
4. Use funder_search to identify research funding patterns in a field

For tracking research trends:
1. Use get_categories to identify relevant subject areas
2. Use search_preprints with date filters for recent activity
3. Use get_statistics to understand submission volumes

## plugin:bio-research:c-trials
An MCP server for accessing ClinicalTrials.gov API v2.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search trials by condition, intervention, location, sponsor, status, and eligibility
- Data Access: Comprehensive clinical trial data from the NIH/NLM registry

ClinicalTrials.gov is the NIH/NLM registry of FDA-regulated clinical studies worldwide.
This server enables:
- Competitive intelligence and pipeline analysis
- Patient recruitment strategies and trial matching
- Investigator site selection and network building
- Protocol design research and endpoint analysis
- Evidence generation for payer negotiations and market access

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_trials: Primary tool for finding trials by condition, intervention, location, or status
• get_trial_details: Deep dive into a specific trial's protocol, endpoints, and locations
• search_by_sponsor: Company/institution pipeline analysis and competitive intelligence
• search_investigators: Find principal investigators and research sites - essential for investigator verification
• analyze_endpoints: Systematic endpoint comparison across trials - use for protocol design and benchmark analysis
• search_by_eligibility: Match patients to trials based on demographic and clinical criteria

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive trial analysis, combine multiple tools:
1. Start with search_trials to find relevant trials by condition/intervention
2. Use get_trial_details for each trial requiring deeper analysis
3. Use analyze_endpoints to systematically compare outcome measures across similar trials
4. Use search_investigators to identify key opinion leaders and active research sites

For investigator verification:
1. Use search_investigators with condition and location to find PIs
2. Extract investigator names from results

Use this server to access comprehensive data on clinical trials including study design,
eligibility criteria, enrollment information, outcome measures, locations, and results.

## plugin:bio-research:chembl
An MCP server for accessing the EMBL-EBI ChEMBL Database v34.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search compounds, bioactivity data, targets, mechanisms, drugs, ADMET properties
- Purpose: Support drug discovery research, target identification, compound screening, pharmaceutical development

ChEMBL is a manually curated database of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties.
It contains compound structures, bioactivity data against biological targets, and
drug mechanism information. The database integrates data from medicinal chemistry literature,
patents, and screening experiments.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• compound_search: Find compounds by name, SMILES, or ChEMBL ID - starting point for compound analysis
• target_search: Find biological targets (proteins, genes, receptors) - essential for understanding drug mechanisms
• get_bioactivity: Retrieve IC50, EC50, Ki values - quantitative activity data for compound-target pairs
• get_mechanism: Get mechanism of action and target binding - explains HOW a drug works
• drug_search: Find approved drugs by indication or name - for therapeutic landscape analysis
• get_admet: Retrieve ADMET properties - pharmacokinetic and safety predictions

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive drug analysis, combine multiple tools:
1. Start with compound_search or drug_search to identify the compound of interest
2. Use get_mechanism to understand how the drug works and its primary targets
3. Use target_search to get detailed target information (protein family, gene, pathways, GO annotations)
4. Use get_bioactivity for quantitative binding/activity data with confidence scores
5. Use get_admet for pharmacokinetic properties

For target-based analysis:
1. Use target_search to find targets by gene symbol or protein name
2. Use get_bioactivity with target_chembl_id to find active compounds
3. Use compound_search to get details on promising compounds

Key capabilities:
- Search compounds by name, structure (SMILES), or ChEMBL ID
- Retrieve bioactivity data (IC50, EC50, Ki values) with confidence scores
- Query biological targets (proteins, enzymes, receptors) by name or gene symbol
- Access drug mechanism of action and target interactions
- Find approved drugs and clinical candidates by indication
- Get ADMET-related molecular properties

Example queries:
• "Find bioactivity data for aspirin"
• "What are the known targets for compound CHEMBL25?"
• "Search for kinase inhibitors with IC50 < 100nM"
• "What drugs target the EGFR protein?"
• "Find approved drugs for treating hypertension"
• "What are the ADMET properties of imatinib?"

## plugin:bio-research:consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: Some search results end with a sign-up, upgrade, or usage message. When a result has one, you MUST include it at the END of your response word-for-word: do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. When a result has none, do not add one: never write your own upgrade prompt, search count, or Consensus link. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. For a broad request (a review, screening, finding everything on a topic), make one search with a large page_size rather than many narrower searches. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

## plugin:browser-use:browser-use
# This MCP server

These rules override the skill below where they differ:
- Code runs in browser_exec; there is no shell, so ignore `BU_NAME=... browser-use <<'PY'` examples.
- Local: without a cloud browser, browser_exec drives the user's own Chrome; where none can be attached (no Chrome installed, Linux with no display, or remote debugging off in Chrome) its own Chromium on a temp profile instead. The first browser_exec result says which, and how to get the user's Chrome.
- Cloud: `start_remote_daemon()` (call browser_login first if not signed in). Every later browser_exec and
  browser_screenshot drives that cloud browser; never pass BU_NAME. One cloud browser per server, under a name only it
  uses: a name passed to start_remote_daemon / stop_remote_daemon is ignored.
- It lives 30 minutes unless you pass `timeout=<minutes>` (up to 240), and this server stops it when it
  exits. Once it ends, calls fail with an error: start a new one, never fall back to the local Chrome.
- Code runs in this server's process: it can read the server's environment (BROWSER_USE_API_KEY when set) and files.
- The live view and CDP URLs grant control of the browser, so they are not shown. Only if the user asks to watch, run
  `os.environ["BH_OPEN_LIVE_URL"] = "1"` before start_remote_daemon: the live view then opens in their browser, and
  both are returned.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, run `browser-use --doctor` and follow its output and the error message.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background; call `activate_tab(target)` only when the user explicitly asks
  or a page demonstrably pauses rendering while hidden.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.

Details for agents go here.

1	# SMA-767: a stripped macOS binding that dyld rejects (mis-aligned LINKEDIT string pool)
2	
3	Status: approved by Sven at GATE 1 (2026-11-13). Linear: SMA-767.
4	Branch: `feature/sma-767-maturin-linkedit-dlopen`.
5	
6	## 1. Problem
7	
8	On the development Mac, `import paigasus_py_bindings` fails for every local maturin build:
9	
10	```
11	dlopen(...paigasus_py_bindings.abi3.so, 0x0002): ... (mis-aligned LINKEDIT string pool, fileOffset=0x00062514)
12	```
13	
14	So `moon run paigasus-kernel-py:test` fails locally (rc 2). CI (Linux) is not affected, because
15	Linux uses ELF, not Mach-O.
16	
17	## 2. Measured cause
18	
19	All facts in this section are MEASURED on 2026-11-13 on the development Mac, unless a line says
20	"inferred". §9 lists the scripts.
21	
22	Host: macOS 27.2 (build 26B123), arm64. Command Line Tools SDK 27.2, `ld-27106.1`, Apple clang
23	21.0.0. Rust 1.95.0 (LLVM 22.1.2), maturin 1.9.6, MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET 11.0 (set by maturin).
24	
25	### 2.1 The chain
26	
27	1. The workspace has no `[profile.release]`. So a release build uses the cargo default
28	   `strip = "debuginfo"`. `cargo build --release -v` passes `-C strip=debuginfo` to 26 of the
29	   rustc units, including every build script and proc macro. A dev build passes it to none
30	   (0 of 34 units). So the defect concerns release builds only.
31	2. On macOS, rustc 1.95 does that strip with its bundled `rust-objcopy` (LLVM), not with Apple
32	   `strip`. Proof: a cloned toolchain with a logging wrapper in place of `rust-objcopy`. The log
33	   shows `rust-objcopy --strip-debug <target>/release/deps/libpaigasus_py_bindings.dylib`. It also
34	   shows the same call for 8 build scripts and 2 proc-macro dylibs.
35	3. `rust-objcopy` writes the LINKEDIT tables back to back with no padding: the symbol table
36	   (16-byte entries), then the indirect symbol table (4-byte entries), then the string pool.
37	4. The py dylib has 215 indirect symbols, an odd count. So the string pool starts on a 4-byte
38	   boundary: `symoff 381176 + 1292 × 16 = 401848 = indirectsymoff`; `401848 + 215 × 4 = 402708 =
39	   stroff = 0x62514`. 402708 mod 8 = 4.
40	5. dyld on macOS 27.2 rejects a string pool that is not 8-byte aligned, but only in a binary whose
41	   `LC_BUILD_VERSION` `sdk` field is new. The same mis-aligned bytes, stamped with `vtool` and
42	   re-signed: `sdk 27.2` is rejected; `sdk 26.5` and `sdk 15.0` load. Every local build has
43	   `sdk 27.2`, because the host SDK is 27.2.
44	6. maturin does not change the file. The cargo dylib and the `.so` in the wheel are
45	   byte-identical (`shasum` equal).
46	
47	ld64 itself (no strip step) pads the string pool: `434808 + 860 = 435668`, but `stroff = 435672`.
48	
49	### 2.2 The matrix (all local, `sdk 27.2`)
50	
51	| Build | stroff | mod 8 | Load |
52	|---|---|---|---|
53	| maturin `--release`, fresh `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
54	| cargo release, default strip | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
55	| cargo release, `strip = "symbols"` | 383876 | 4 | rejected |
56	| cargo release, `strip = "none"` | 435672 | 0 | loads |
57	| cargo debug (no strip) | 807032 | 0 | loads |
58	| release, MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET 12.0 / 27.0 / unset | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
59	| unstripped dylib + Apple `/usr/bin/strip -S` | 402712 | 0 | loads |
60	| unstripped dylib + Apple `/usr/bin/strip -x` | 383896 | 0 | loads |
61	| unstripped dylib + `rust-objcopy --strip-debug` | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
62	| unstripped dylib + `rust-objcopy --strip-all` | 383844 | 4 | rejected |
63	| maturin + `-C strip=none` as an apple-darwin target rustflag | 435672 | 0 | loads |
64	| napi binding, cargo release, default strip | 470128 | 0 | loads (198 indirect symbols, even) |
65	| napi binding, cargo release, `strip = "none"` | 503056 | 0 | loads |
66	
67	In every build, `stroff mod 8 = 4` with `sdk 27.2` failed to load, and `stroff mod 8 = 0` loaded.
68	
69	### 2.3 Candidate causes from the issue, and the verdict
70	
71	- **Stale or huge `rs/target`**: ruled out. A fresh `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` in a scratch directory
72	  fails at the same offset `0x00062514`.
73	- **macOS SDK / linker against Rust 1.95**: the linker is not at fault. The ld64 output loads.
74	  The fault is the post-link strip tool (`rust-objcopy`). The SDK matters only because dyld
75	  enforces the rule for a binary linked with the new SDK (§2.1.5).
76	- **The napi binding on the same host**: its release build loads, but only by chance (198 is
77	  even). Its dev build, which `paigasus-kernel-ts:build` uses, is never stripped.
78	- **Deployment target**: not a factor.
79	
80	### 2.4 The published artefacts and CI
81	
82	Inspected with `otool` only. The downloads were not executed.
83	
84	| Artefact | sdk | indirect syms | stroff | mod 8 |
85	|---|---|---|---|---|
86	| PyPI `paigasus-py-bindings` 0.2.0, `macosx_11_0_arm64` | 26.5 | 215 | 402428 | 4 |
87	| PyPI `paigasus-py-bindings` 0.2.0, `macosx_10_12_x86_64` | 26.5 | 215 | 397956 | 4 |
88	| npm `@paigasus/node-bindings-darwin-arm64` 0.2.0 | 26.5 | 192 | 435872 | 0 |
89	
90	- The two PyPI wheels are mis-aligned, but they carry `sdk 26.5`. By §2.1.5 they load on macOS 27
91	  (inferred: the same rule held for a stamped local file; the wheels themselves were not loaded).
92	- CI is green because the CI runners link with SDK 26.5 (inferred from the artefacts). When the
93	  runner image moves to SDK 27, the published macOS wheels will stop loading on macOS 27. Today
94	  this is a latent defect for users, and an active defect for local builds.
95	- `@paigasus/node-bindings-darwin-x64` 0.2.0 was not inspected.
96	- Upstream (not verified): a web search found LLVM commit #203680, "[llvm-objcopy][MachO] Align
97	  __LINKEDIT entries to pointer size". I did not read it. I do not know which Rust release
98	  contains it.
99	
100	## 3. Decisions
101	
102	- **D1. Fix: add `-C strip=none` to the apple-darwin rustflags in `rs/.cargo/config.toml`.** Both
103	  triples (`x86_64-apple-darwin`, `aarch64-apple-darwin`) already have a `rustflags` list there.
104	  Append `"-C", "strip=none"` to each. rustc gets the profile's `-C strip=debuginfo` first and the
105	  rustflag last, and the last one wins (measured in the `-v` log). Measured: the maturin wheel
106	  built this way loads (row in §2.2). That measurement used the env form of the key
107	  (`CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_APPLE_DARWIN_RUSTFLAGS`), not an edit of the file. The real Moon task
108	  with the edited file is not measured yet (§6 step 1).
109	
110	  Why this place:
111	  - It applies only to macOS builds. A profile override cannot be limited to one target. Measured
112	    in a `rust:1.95.0-bookworm` container: `strip = "none"` grows the Linux py `.so` from 582072 to
113	    4488136 bytes (7.7 times), and the Linux napi `.so` from 671056 to 4577928 bytes. On macOS the
114	    growth is +39 KB (508112 to 547600), because Mach-O keeps DWARF out of the dylib.
115	  - It covers both bindings with one change: maturin, `uv` (PEP 517), and `napi build` all run
116	    cargo from inside `rs/`. The `wheels.yml` darwin legs run maturin with `working-directory: rs`
117	    and set no `RUSTFLAGS` (only the musl leg does).
118	  - In a release build without `--target`, it also reaches the build scripts and proc macros
119	    (the rustflag appears on the build-script rustc lines in the `-v` log). This covers R1 for
120	    local builds.
121	  - The CI darwin legs pass `--target`. Then the rustflag reaches only the target units, not the
122	    host build scripts and proc macros. That is acceptable while CI links with SDK 26.5.
123	
124	  Rejected:
125	  - `[profile.release.package.<binding>] strip = "none"` in `rs/Cargo.toml`. Measured to work on
126	    all paths, and the sdist carries it. Rejected because of the 7.7 times Linux growth above.
127	  - `[tool.maturin] rustc-args` in the binding's `pyproject.toml`. Measured to work. Rejected: it
128	    applies to every platform (same Linux growth) and does not cover the napi binding.
129	  - A workspace-wide `[profile.release] strip = "none"`. Same Linux cost, and it changes every
130	    service binary and container image.
131	  - Strip with Apple `strip` after the build. It loads, but cargo has no stable hook. Each build
132	    path would need its own post-step.
133	  - A newer Rust toolchain. No release with a known fix (§2.4).
134	  - A documented workaround only. A cheap repo-local fix exists.
135	
136	- **D2. The sdist gap.** maturin does not ship `rs/.cargo/config.toml` in the sdist (SMA-578).
137	  So a user who builds the sdist on a host with SDK 27 gets a binary that does not load.
138	  Decided by Sven (P1). The plan first measures one option: ship a `.cargo/config.toml`
139	  at the sdist root with `[tool.maturin] include` (`format = "sdist"`), then build from the
140	  extracted sdist and import. If that works, adopt it and add the D3 guard to the macOS leg of
141	  `sdist-verify`. If it does not work, accept the gap as a residual, and document the sdist
142	  workaround (`CARGO_TARGET_<TRIPLE>_RUSTFLAGS="-C strip=none"` or `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none`
143	  for the build) in `py/README.md` and in the `rs/.cargo/config.toml` comment.
144	
145	  MEASURED after GATE 1: `include = [{ path = "../../../.cargo/config.toml", … }]` fails
146	  ("paths in archives must not have `..`"). An include path is relative to the crate directory
147	  and lands at the same path under the sdist root. So a crate-local
148	  `rs/crates/bindings/paigasus-py-bindings/.cargo/config.toml` that holds only the strip flag lands
149	  at the sdist root. A wheel built from that extracted sdist (outside the repo, Rust 1.95.0) has
150	  `stroff 435672` and loads, with 0 build warnings. Decision: ship it (P1). Cost: a second config
151	  file, which cargo merges with `rs/.cargo/config.toml` when the cwd is the crate directory.
152	
153	- **D3. CI guard.** Add an assertion to the darwin steps that exist today:
154	  - `wheels.yml`, step "Assert Mach-O arch and minimum macOS (darwin only)": each `*.abi3.so`.
155	  - `prebuild.yml`, step "Verify Mach-O architecture (darwin only)": both `.node` files.
156	
157	  The parse must not use a pipe into a reader that exits early (`repo:actionlint` check 13). Use
158	  the idiom that the minos parse already uses:
159	  `otool -l "$f" | awk '/^ *stroff /&&!d{v=$2; d=1} END{print v}'`. Check that the value has only
160	  digits with `case`. Fail when the value is empty, not numeric, or `stroff mod 8 ≠ 0`. The error
161	  names SMA-767. The guard is needed because the runner's binaries carry `sdk 26.5`, so dyld on
162	  the runner does not check, and the import step cannot catch a regression.
163	
164	  P3 (decided by Sven): check `stroff` mod 8 only, with a proof that it bites (D4). If more fields are checked later, use a
165	  per-field rule (`stroff` and `symoff` mod 8, `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE` `dataoff` mod 16), never one
166	  rule for every `*off` field.
167	
168	- **D4. The guard must bite.** Before the merge, run the exact D3 text from both workflows,
169	  statically, against:
170	  - the unfixed local dylib (`stroff 402708`): must fail;
171	  - the PyPI 0.2.0 arm64 and x86_64 wheels: must fail;
172	  - the npm darwin-arm64 0.2.0 `.node`: must pass;
173	  - a file with no `LC_SYMTAB` (for example a text file): must fail;
174	  - the fixed local dylib: must pass.
175	  Record all outputs in the PR.
176	
177	- **D5. Records.**
178	  - A comment in `rs/.cargo/config.toml` next to the new flag: the cause, the measurement, the
179	    SDK gate, and the removal condition (D6).
180	  - One entry in `rs/CLAUDE.md`: do not remove the flag until D6 holds; do not add maturin
181	    `--strip`/`strip = true` or napi `--strip`, because each one runs `rust-objcopy` again; a
182	    "mis-aligned LINKEDIT" error on macOS means a `rust-objcopy`-stripped Mach-O with a new SDK.
183	  - A short note in `py/README.md`: after you pull this change, run the "After a Rust change"
184	    command once. The shared `py/.venv` keeps the broken binding until then, because uv's cache
185	    key for the binding does not include `rs/.cargo/config.toml` (inferred from uv's default cache
186	    keys, not measured). Also a pointer to the `rs/CLAUDE.md` entry.
187	  - A pointer in the wheels bullet of `.github/CLAUDE.md`, next to the other Mach-O assertions.
188	
189	- **D6. Removal condition.** Remove the flag only when the pinned toolchain's `rust-objcopy` pads
190	  the string pool. Test it on a dylib with an odd indirect symbol count:
191	  `stroff > indirectsymoff + 4 × nindirectsyms`. The D3 guard alone cannot prove it, because an
192	  even count passes by chance.
193	
194	- **D7. No version bump and no re-release.** Decided by Sven (P4). R6 records the inference. The published 0.2.0
195	  wheels load on macOS 27 today (inferred, §2.4). The next normal release ships aligned wheels.
196	  The commit type is `fix(rs)`. `rs/.cargo/config.toml` is outside every crate directory, so
197	  release-plz probably sees no package change (inferred; the plan must confirm it).
198	
199	- **D8. Rollback.** Revert D1 and D3 together. A revert of D1 alone makes the D3 guard red on
200	  the next odd count.
201	
202	## 4. Goals and non-goals
203	
204	Goals:
205	- `moon run paigasus-kernel-py:test` passes on the development Mac (macOS 27.2).
206	- Local release builds of both bindings load on this Mac.
207	- CI fails when a darwin binding has a mis-aligned string pool, before the runner SDK moves to 27.
208	
209	Non-goals:
210	- A fix for `rust-objcopy`, or a report upstream.
211	- A change to Linux or Windows artefacts, service binaries, container images, or the wasm binding.
212	- A local Moon gate for this alignment. The local import already fails loudly.
213	
214	Anti-goals:
215	- A fix that grows the Linux wheels or prebuilds.
216	- A fix that works only through maturin and leaves `cargo build --release` broken.
217	
218	## 5. Affected-graph cost
219	
220	`rs/.cargo/config.toml` is a task input for 61 tasks (`rs/CLAUDE.md`, A10). The PR selects them in
221	`moon ci`. Both `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml` list `rs/.cargo/config.toml` in their
222	`pull_request` paths, so the PR runs both guards before the merge. `images.yml` does not list it.
223	The `.github/workflows/*` edits select `repo:actionlint` and the other workflow gates.
224	
225	## 6. Verification for the plan
226	
227	1. `moon run paigasus-kernel-py:test --force` on the Mac: rc 0.
228	2. `napi build --platform --release` for the napi crate on the Mac: `stroff` must be the
229	   unstripped value (503056 at the time of writing), not 470128. The count is even, so alignment
230	   alone cannot show the effect.
231	3. D4, all five cases.
232	4. The "After a Rust change" command from `py/README.md`, then `moon run py:test` on the Mac: rc 0.
233	5. If P1 adopts the sdist option: a wheel built from the extracted sdist outside the repo loads.
234	   Read its build log for cargo warnings.
235	6. Read the CI artefact sizes from this PR's `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml` runs. Linux and
236	   Windows sizes must not change against `main`.
237	7. `nm -ap <CI darwin .so> | grep OSO`: record the paths (R3).
238	8. The full gate graph from the root `CLAUDE.md` before the push. Read the gate notes on bash
239	   versions for this Mac.
240	
241	## 7. Decisions by Sven (GATE 1, 2026-11-13)
242	
243	Sven approved the spec at GATE 1 and decided the four provisional calls:
244	
245	- **P1.** Measure `[tool.maturin] include` for `.cargo/config.toml` in the sdist, and test a build
246	  from that sdist. If it works, ship it and add the sdist guard. If it does not work, record the
247	  gap as an accepted residual, with the sdist workaround in the docs.
248	- **P2.** The fix is the macOS-only rustflag `-C strip=none` in the apple-darwin `rustflags` of
249	  `rs/.cargo/config.toml`.
250	- **P3.** The CI guard checks only `stroff` alignment (mod 8), with a proof that it bites.
251	- **P4.** No extra release for 0.2.0. The inference about 0.2.0 is a residual (R6).
252	
253	## 8. Risks and residuals
254	
255	- **R1.** Proc macros and build scripts in a release build with `--target` are still stripped by
256	  `rust-objcopy`. rustc `dlopen`s the proc macros. Today all of them are aligned (2 proc-macro
257	  dylibs, 8 build scripts, measured). The CI darwin legs use `--target` and SDK 26.5, so they are
258	  not at risk today. Local builds without `--target` are covered by D1.
259	- **R2.** The guard runs in `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml`. A PR that edits only
260	  `rs/.cargo/config.toml` runs both before the merge. A PR that edits only binding source does
261	  not, but `release.yml` calls both workflows, and `approve-release` needs them. So every publish
262	  is gated.
263	- **R3.** The unstripped darwin `.so` keeps 4 N_OSO debug-map entries. Each holds the absolute
264	  path of a `std` rlib under the builder's rustup home (locally `/Users/<home>/.rustup/...`; in CI
265	  `/Users/runner/...`). No personal data ships from CI. The build is less reproducible.
266	- **R4.** A user who installs the sdist on a host with SDK 27 (for example PyPy) gets a broken
267	  binary, unless P1 closes the gap.
268	- **R6.** The published 0.2.0 macOS wheels are mis-aligned. That they load on macOS 27 is an
269	  inference from the `sdk 26.5` stamp test (§2.4); nobody loaded them. No extra release (P4).
270	- **R5.** The shared `py/.venv` of every Mac checkout keeps the broken binding until the README
271	  command runs (D5).
272	
273	## 9. Measurement scripts
274	
275	The scripts lived in a scratch directory under `$TMPDIR` (`sma767.*`). They are not in the repo.
276	
277	- `matrix.sh`: cargo build per row (`CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP`, `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`),
278	  copy the dylib to `paigasus_py_bindings.abi3.so`, read `stroff` with `otool -l`, import it.
279	- `manual.sh`: run Apple `strip` and `rust-objcopy` by hand on the unstripped dylib, then import.
280	- `wrap.sh`: `cp -Rc` the toolchain, replace `rust-objcopy` with a logger, build with `RUSTC` set.
281	- `sdk.sh`: `vtool -set-build-version macos 11.0 <sdk> -replace`, `codesign -f -s -`, import.
282	- `rflag.sh`: `CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_APPLE_DARWIN_RUSTFLAGS` (the env form of the config key)
283	  with `-C strip=none` appended, maturin build, import.
284	- `linux.sh`: in `rust:1.95.0-bookworm`, release build with `strip` `debuginfo` and `none`, size.
285	- `fix.sh`, `sdist.sh`, `moontask.sh`: apply each profile-based candidate, build, import, restore
286	  the file with `git checkout --`.
287

# SMA-767: a stripped macOS binding that dyld rejects (mis-aligned LINKEDIT string pool)

Status: approved by Sven at GATE 1 (2026-11-13). Linear: SMA-767.
Branch: `feature/sma-767-maturin-linkedit-dlopen`.

## 1. Problem

On the development Mac, `import paigasus_py_bindings` fails for every local maturin build:

```
dlopen(...paigasus_py_bindings.abi3.so, 0x0002): ... (mis-aligned LINKEDIT string pool, fileOffset=0x00062514)
```

So `moon run paigasus-kernel-py:test` fails locally (rc 2). CI (Linux) is not affected, because
Linux uses ELF, not Mach-O.

## 2. Measured cause

All facts in this section are MEASURED on 2026-11-13 on the development Mac, unless a line says
"inferred". §9 lists the scripts.

Host: macOS 27.2 (build 26B123), arm64. Command Line Tools SDK 27.2, `ld-27106.1`, Apple clang
21.0.0. Rust 1.95.0 (LLVM 22.1.2), maturin 1.9.6, MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET 11.0 (set by maturin).

### 2.1 The chain

1. The workspace has no `[profile.release]`. So a release build uses the cargo default
   `strip = "debuginfo"`. `cargo build --release -v` passes `-C strip=debuginfo` to 26 of the
   rustc units, including every build script and proc macro. A dev build passes it to none
   (0 of 34 units). So the defect concerns release builds only.
2. On macOS, rustc 1.95 does that strip with its bundled `rust-objcopy` (LLVM), not with Apple
   `strip`. Proof: a cloned toolchain with a logging wrapper in place of `rust-objcopy`. The log
   shows `rust-objcopy --strip-debug <target>/release/deps/libpaigasus_py_bindings.dylib`. It also
   shows the same call for 8 build scripts and 2 proc-macro dylibs.
3. `rust-objcopy` writes the LINKEDIT tables back to back with no padding: the symbol table
   (16-byte entries), then the indirect symbol table (4-byte entries), then the string pool.
4. The py dylib has 215 indirect symbols, an odd count. So the string pool starts on a 4-byte
   boundary: `symoff 381176 + 1292 × 16 = 401848 = indirectsymoff`; `401848 + 215 × 4 = 402708 =
   stroff = 0x62514`. 402708 mod 8 = 4.
5. dyld on macOS 27.2 rejects a string pool that is not 8-byte aligned, but only in a binary whose
   `LC_BUILD_VERSION` `sdk` field is new. The same mis-aligned bytes, stamped with `vtool` and
   re-signed: `sdk 27.2` is rejected; `sdk 26.5` and `sdk 15.0` load. Every local build has
   `sdk 27.2`, because the host SDK is 27.2.
6. maturin does not change the file. The cargo dylib and the `.so` in the wheel are
   byte-identical (`shasum` equal).

ld64 itself (no strip step) pads the string pool: `434808 + 860 = 435668`, but `stroff = 435672`.

| Build | stroff | mod 8 | Load |
|---|---|---|---|
| maturin `--release`, fresh `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
| cargo release, default strip | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
| cargo release, `strip = "symbols"` | 383876 | 4 | rejected |
| cargo release, `strip = "none"` | 435672 | 0 | loads |
| cargo debug (no strip) | 807032 | 0 | loads |
| release, MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET 12.0 / 27.0 / unset | 402708 | 4 | rejected |
| unstripped dylib + Apple `/usr/bin/strip -S` | 402712 | 0 | loads |
| unstripped dylib + Apple `/usr/bin/strip -x` | 383896 | 0 | loads |

In every build, `stroff mod 8 = 4` with `sdk 27.2` failed to load, and `stroff mod 8 = 0` loaded.

### 2.3 Candidate causes from the issue, and the verdict

- **Stale or huge `rs/target`**: ruled out. A fresh `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` in a scratch directory
  fails at the same offset `0x00062514`.
- **macOS SDK / linker against Rust 1.95**: the linker is not at fault. The ld64 output loads.
  The fault is the post-link strip tool (`rust-objcopy`). The SDK matters only because dyld
  enforces the rule for a binary linked with the new SDK (§2.1.5).
- **The napi binding on the same host**: its release build loads, but only by chance (198 is
  even). Its dev build, which `paigasus-kernel-ts:build` uses, is never stripped.
- **Deployment target**: not a factor.

### 2.4 The published artefacts and CI

Inspected with `otool` only. The downloads were not executed.

| Artefact | sdk | indirect syms | stroff | mod 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PyPI `paigasus-py-bindings` 0.2.0, `macosx_11_0_arm64` | 26.5 | 215 | 402428 | 4 |
| PyPI `paigasus-py-bindings` 0.2.0, `macosx_10_12_x86_64` | 26.5 | 215 | 397956 | 4 |
| npm `@paigasus/node-bindings-darwin-arm64` 0.2.0 | 26.5 | 192 | 435872 | 0 |

- The two PyPI wheels are mis-aligned, but they carry `sdk 26.5`. By §2.1.5 they load on macOS 27
  (inferred: the same rule held for a stamped local file; the wheels themselves were not loaded).
- CI is green because the CI runners link with SDK 26.5 (inferred from the artefacts). When the
  runner image moves to SDK 27, the published macOS wheels will stop loading on macOS 27. Today
  this is a latent defect for users, and an active defect for local builds.
- `@paigasus/node-bindings-darwin-x64` 0.2.0 was not inspected.
- Upstream (not verified): a web search found LLVM commit #203680, "[llvm-objcopy][MachO] Align
  __LINKEDIT entries to pointer size". I did not read it. I do not know which Rust release
  contains it.

## 3. Decisions

- **D1. Fix: add `-C strip=none` to the apple-darwin rustflags in `rs/.cargo/config.toml`.** Both
  triples (`x86_64-apple-darwin`, `aarch64-apple-darwin`) already have a `rustflags` list there.
  Append `"-C", "strip=none"` to each. rustc gets the profile's `-C strip=debuginfo` first and the
  rustflag last, and the last one wins (measured in the `-v` log). Measured: the maturin wheel
  built this way loads (row in §2.2). That measurement used the env form of the key
  (`CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_APPLE_DARWIN_RUSTFLAGS`), not an edit of the file. The real Moon task
  with the edited file is not measured yet (§6 step 1).

  Why this place:
  - It applies only to macOS builds. A profile override cannot be limited to one target. Measured
    in a `rust:1.95.0-bookworm` container: `strip = "none"` grows the Linux py `.so` from 582072 to
    4488136 bytes (7.7 times), and the Linux napi `.so` from 671056 to 4577928 bytes. On macOS the
    growth is +39 KB (508112 to 547600), because Mach-O keeps DWARF out of the dylib.
  - It covers both bindings with one change: maturin, `uv` (PEP 517), and `napi build` all run
    cargo from inside `rs/`. The `wheels.yml` darwin legs run maturin with `working-directory: rs`
    and set no `RUSTFLAGS` (only the musl leg does).
  - In a release build without `--target`, it also reaches the build scripts and proc macros
    (the rustflag appears on the build-script rustc lines in the `-v` log). This covers R1 for
    local builds.
  - The CI darwin legs pass `--target`. Then the rustflag reaches only the target units, not the
    host build scripts and proc macros. That is acceptable while CI links with SDK 26.5.

  Rejected:
  - `[profile.release.package.<binding>] strip = "none"` in `rs/Cargo.toml`. Measured to work on
    all paths, and the sdist carries it. Rejected because of the 7.7 times Linux growth above.
  - `[tool.maturin] rustc-args` in the binding's `pyproject.toml`. Measured to work. Rejected: it
    applies to every platform (same Linux growth) and does not cover the napi binding.
  - A workspace-wide `[profile.release] strip = "none"`. Same Linux cost, and it changes every
    service binary and container image.
  - Strip with Apple `strip` after the build. It loads, but cargo has no stable hook. Each build
    path would need its own post-step.
  - A newer Rust toolchain. No release with a known fix (§2.4).
  - A documented workaround only. A cheap repo-local fix exists.

- **D2. The sdist gap.** maturin does not ship `rs/.cargo/config.toml` in the sdist (SMA-578).
  So a user who builds the sdist on a host with SDK 27 gets a binary that does not load.
  Decided by Sven (P1). The plan first measures one option: ship a `.cargo/config.toml`
  at the sdist root with `[tool.maturin] include` (`format = "sdist"`), then build from the
  extracted sdist and import. If that works, adopt it and add the D3 guard to the macOS leg of
  `sdist-verify`. If it does not work, accept the gap as a residual, and document the sdist
  workaround (`CARGO_TARGET_<TRIPLE>_RUSTFLAGS="-C strip=none"` or `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none`
  for the build) in `py/README.md` and in the `rs/.cargo/config.toml` comment.

  MEASURED after GATE 1: `include = [{ path = "../../../.cargo/config.toml", … }]` fails
  ("paths in archives must not have `..`"). An include path is relative to the crate directory
  and lands at the same path under the sdist root. So a crate-local
  `rs/crates/bindings/paigasus-py-bindings/.cargo/config.toml` that holds only the strip flag lands
  at the sdist root. A wheel built from that extracted sdist (outside the repo, Rust 1.95.0) has
  `stroff 435672` and loads, with 0 build warnings. Decision: ship it (P1). Cost: a second config
  file, which cargo merges with `rs/.cargo/config.toml` when the cwd is the crate directory.

- **D3. CI guard.** Add an assertion to the darwin steps that exist today:
  - `wheels.yml`, step "Assert Mach-O arch and minimum macOS (darwin only)": each `*.abi3.so`.
  - `prebuild.yml`, step "Verify Mach-O architecture (darwin only)": both `.node` files.

  The parse must not use a pipe into a reader that exits early (`repo:actionlint` check 13). Use
  the idiom that the minos parse already uses:
  `otool -l "$f" | awk '/^ *stroff /&&!d{v=$2; d=1} END{print v}'`. Check that the value has only
  digits with `case`. Fail when the value is empty, not numeric, or `stroff mod 8 ≠ 0`. The error
  names SMA-767. The guard is needed because the runner's binaries carry `sdk 26.5`, so dyld on
  the runner does not check, and the import step cannot catch a regression.

  P3 (decided by Sven): check `stroff` mod 8 only, with a proof that it bites (D4). If more fields are checked later, use a
  per-field rule (`stroff` and `symoff` mod 8, `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE` `dataoff` mod 16), never one
  rule for every `*off` field.

- **D4. The guard must bite.** Before the merge, run the exact D3 text from both workflows,
  statically, against:
  - the unfixed local dylib (`stroff 402708`): must fail;
  - the PyPI 0.2.0 arm64 and x86_64 wheels: must fail;
  - the npm darwin-arm64 0.2.0 `.node`: must pass;
  - a file with no `LC_SYMTAB` (for example a text file): must fail;
  - the fixed local dylib: must pass.
  Record all outputs in the PR.

- **D5. Records.**
  - A comment in `rs/.cargo/config.toml` next to the new flag: the cause, the measurement, the
    SDK gate, and the removal condition (D6).
  - One entry in `rs/CLAUDE.md`: do not remove the flag until D6 holds; do not add maturin
    `--strip`/`strip = true` or napi `--strip`, because each one runs `rust-objcopy` again; a
    "mis-aligned LINKEDIT" error on macOS means a `rust-objcopy`-stripped Mach-O with a new SDK.
  - A short note in `py/README.md`: after you pull this change, run the "After a Rust change"
    command once. The shared `py/.venv` keeps the broken binding until then, because uv's cache
    key for the binding does not include `rs/.cargo/config.toml` (inferred from uv's default cache
    keys, not measured). Also a pointer to the `rs/CLAUDE.md` entry.
  - A pointer in the wheels bullet of `.github/CLAUDE.md`, next to the other Mach-O assertions.

- **D6. Removal condition.** Remove the flag only when the pinned toolchain's `rust-objcopy` pads
  the string pool. Test it on a dylib with an odd indirect symbol count:
  `stroff > indirectsymoff + 4 × nindirectsyms`. The D3 guard alone cannot prove it, because an
  even count passes by chance.

- **D7. No version bump and no re-release.** Decided by Sven (P4). R6 records the inference. The published 0.2.0
  wheels load on macOS 27 today (inferred, §2.4). The next normal release ships aligned wheels.
  The commit type is `fix(rs)`. `rs/.cargo/config.toml` is outside every crate directory, so
  release-plz probably sees no package change (inferred; the plan must confirm it).

- **D8. Rollback.** Revert D1 and D3 together. A revert of D1 alone makes the D3 guard red on
  the next odd count.

## 4. Goals and non-goals

Goals:
- `moon run paigasus-kernel-py:test` passes on the development Mac (macOS 27.2).
- Local release builds of both bindings load on this Mac.
- CI fails when a darwin binding has a mis-aligned string pool, before the runner SDK moves to 27.

Non-goals:
- A fix for `rust-objcopy`, or a report upstream.
- A change to Linux or Windows artefacts, service binaries, container images, or the wasm binding.
- A local Moon gate for this alignment. The local import already fails loudly.

Anti-goals:
- A fix that grows the Linux wheels or prebuilds.
- A fix that works only through maturin and leaves `cargo build --release` broken.

## 5. Affected-graph cost

`rs/.cargo/config.toml` is a task input for 61 tasks (`rs/CLAUDE.md`, A10). The PR selects them in
`moon ci`. Both `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml` list `rs/.cargo/config.toml` in their
`pull_request` paths, so the PR runs both guards before the merge. `images.yml` does not list it.
The `.github/workflows/*` edits select `repo:actionlint` and the other workflow gates.

## 6. Verification for the plan

1. `moon run paigasus-kernel-py:test --force` on the Mac: rc 0.
2. `napi build --platform --release` for the napi crate on the Mac: `stroff` must be the
   unstripped value (503056 at the time of writing), not 470128. The count is even, so alignment
   alone cannot show the effect.
3. D4, all five cases.
4. The "After a Rust change" command from `py/README.md`, then `moon run py:test` on the Mac: rc 0.
5. If P1 adopts the sdist option: a wheel built from the extracted sdist outside the repo loads.
   Read its build log for cargo warnings.
6. Read the CI artefact sizes from this PR's `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml` runs. Linux and
   Windows sizes must not change against `main`.
7. `nm -ap <CI darwin .so> | grep OSO`: record the paths (R3).
8. The full gate graph from the root `CLAUDE.md` before the push. Read the gate notes on bash
   versions for this Mac.

## 7. Decisions by Sven (GATE 1, 2026-11-13)

Sven approved the spec at GATE 1 and decided the four provisional calls:

- **P1.** Measure `[tool.maturin] include` for `.cargo/config.toml` in the sdist, and test a build
  from that sdist. If it works, ship it and add the sdist guard. If it does not work, record the
  gap as an accepted residual, with the sdist workaround in the docs.
- **P2.** The fix is the macOS-only rustflag `-C strip=none` in the apple-darwin `rustflags` of
  `rs/.cargo/config.toml`.
- **P3.** The CI guard checks only `stroff` alignment (mod 8), with a proof that it bites.
- **P4.** No extra release for 0.2.0. The inference about 0.2.0 is a residual (R6).

## 8. Risks and residuals

- **R1.** Proc macros and build scripts in a release build with `--target` are still stripped by
  `rust-objcopy`. rustc `dlopen`s the proc macros. Today all of them are aligned (2 proc-macro
  dylibs, 8 build scripts, measured). The CI darwin legs use `--target` and SDK 26.5, so they are
  not at risk today. Local builds without `--target` are covered by D1.
- **R2.** The guard runs in `wheels.yml` and `prebuild.yml`. A PR that edits only
  `rs/.cargo/config.toml` runs both before the merge. A PR that edits only binding source does
  not, but `release.yml` calls both workflows, and `approve-release` needs them. So every publish
  is gated.
- **R3.** The unstripped darwin `.so` keeps 4 N_OSO debug-map entries. Each holds the absolute
  path of a `std` rlib under the builder's rustup home (locally `/Users/<home>/.rustup/...`; in CI
  `/Users/runner/...`). No personal data ships from CI. The build is less reproducible.
- **R4.** A user who installs the sdist on a host with SDK 27 (for example PyPy) gets a broken
  binary, unless P1 closes the gap.
- **R6.** The published 0.2.0 macOS wheels are mis-aligned. That they load on macOS 27 is an
  inference from the `sdk 26.5` stamp test (§2.4); nobody loaded them. No extra release (P4).
- **R5.** The shared `py/.venv` of every Mac checkout keeps the broken binding until the README
  command runs (D5).

## 9. Measurement scripts

The scripts lived in a scratch directory under `$TMPDIR` (`sma767.*`). They are not in the repo.

- `matrix.sh`: cargo build per row (`CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP`, `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`),
  copy the dylib to `paigasus_py_bindings.abi3.so`, read `stroff` with `otool -l`, import it.
- `manual.sh`: run Apple `strip` and `rust-objcopy` by hand on the unstripped dylib, then import.
- `wrap.sh`: `cp -Rc` the toolchain, replace `rust-objcopy` with a logger, build with `RUSTC` set.
- `sdk.sh`: `vtool -set-build-version macos 11.0 <sdk> -replace`, `codesign -f -s -`, import.
- `rflag.sh`: `CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_APPLE_DARWIN_RUSTFLAGS` (the env form of the config key)
  with `-C strip=none` appended, maturin build, import.
- `linux.sh`: in `rust:1.95.0-bookworm`, release build with `strip` `debuginfo` and `none`, size.
- `fix.sh`, `sdist.sh`, `moontask.sh`: apply each profile-based candidate, build, import, restore
  the file with `git checkout --`.

264	## Workflow linting and shell rules
265	
266	- Workflow trigger filters are gated by `repo:actionlint`. Write `branches:`, `paths:` **and their
267	  `-ignore` variants** as **block sequences**, never the inline `branches: [main]` form — the
268	  gate's extractor does not parse inline flow and fails all four keys loudly rather than skipping
269	  them in silence. Every wildcard-free
270	  `branches:` entry must resolve as `refs/remotes/origin/<name>`; a branch that does not exist yet,
271	  or any entry carrying a glob character (`*`, `?`, `+`, `[]` — `+` included, since GitHub reads it
272	  as a quantifier), needs a justified `BRANCH_SKIP` entry in `ci/actionlint/run.sh`. A typo'd
273	  branch name otherwise disables a workflow silently and permanently (SMA-540).
274	- `ci/actionlint/run.sh`'s check 10 must route **every** exit status of its `release_guard_py`
275	  wrapper, not only the guard's own 2. `run.sh` is `set -uo pipefail` with **no `-e`**, so an
276	  unrouted status leaves `$RG_OUT` empty, the read loop finds nothing and the gate exits 0 having
277	  asserted nothing — measured at rc 127, the status a **missing `uv`** produces from the wrapper
278	  rather than from the guard. Do not read "missing uv aborts the gate" as a property of this
279	  routing: on the full-gate path that abort comes from `release_guard_self_test`'s
280	  `|| infra`. The wrapper also passes `--locked`, so the gate cannot re-lock `py/uv.lock` as a
281	  side effect (SMA-579).
282	- PyYAML coerces five shapes every workflow parser in `ci/` must handle: a bare `on:` key parses
283	  as the boolean `True`; `if: false` and `continue-on-error: false` parse as the boolean `False`;
284	  `continue-on-error: "false"` (quoted) parses as the **string** `"false"`, not the boolean;
285	  `needs:` may be a scalar string rather than a list, and iterating a string in Python yields its
286	  **characters**, not the string itself (SMA-579).
287	- GitHub Actions supports YAML **anchors and aliases** (since 2025-09-18) but **not merge keys**
288	  (`<<:`) — a workflow using one keeps the literal, unmerged key rather than erroring (SMA-579).
289	- `repo:actionlint` now runs shellcheck over every workflow `run:` block, sourced from
290	  `shellcheck-py` pinned in `py/uv.lock` (bounded specifier `>=0.11.0.1,<0.12`), resolved via
291	  `uv run --locked --project py` and asserted with `[ -x ]`. It FAILS CLOSED at rc 2 — there is
292	  deliberately no fallback to whatever `shellcheck` a host happens to have, the silent-downgrade
293	  failure SMA-525 refused. shellcheck's own GitHub release ships 13 platform archives and no
294	  checksums asset (re-measured 2026-09-02), which is why it is not a proto plugin; three of
295	  `shellcheck-py`'s pinned digests were verified by hand against koalaman's release assets, and a
296	  version bump re-opens that check.
297	  **Coverage limit, stated plainly so "the inline bash is linted now" isn't read as more than it
298	  is.** MEASURED: actionlint replaces `${{ }}` expressions with inert placeholders before handing
299	  the script to shellcheck. `rm -rf $TARGET` fires `SC2086`; the structurally identical
300	  `rm -rf ${{ github.event.inputs.target }}` fires nothing. So the entire GitHub-expression
301	  interpolation class — the dominant quoting/injection hazard in `release.yml` and `wheels.yml` —
302	  is uncovered by this gate. zizmor is the tool for that class and runs nowhere in this repo. Also
303	  structural, not a configuration gap: `SC2148` and `SC2164` can never fire, because actionlint
304	  supplies the shell itself and injects `set -e`.
305	- `ci/actionlint/run.sh` check 12 requires a `<!-- moon-diagnosis:ok -->` (or `:superseded`) marker
306	  on ANY file that names `ciReport.json`, unless the file is listed in `CIREPORT_MENTIONS_ALLOWED`.
307	  This is broader than the `doc_diagnosis_self_test` entry above says: it is not only about this
308	  file's own diagnosis procedure block. A new plan or spec that quotes the procedure, or otherwise
309	  mentions `ciReport.json`, reds the gate until it carries the marker or is added to the allowlist.
310	- **A pipe into a reader that can exit early is a false red under `pipefail`** (MEASURED, SMA-647).
311	  `grep -q` stops at its first match. `grep -m N` stops after N matches. `head` stops after N
312	  lines. `awk … exit` stops at its `exit`. Each one stops before it reads the rest of its input. A
313	  producer that writes again after that gets SIGPIPE and exits 141. Under `pipefail` the pipeline
314	  status is then 141, although the reader found the match. On Linux in CI the race is rare and
315	  needs CPU load, so a re-run passes: it caused three false check-12 reds in `repo:actionlint`
316	  (PRs 223, 255, 258). On macOS with BSD grep 2.6.0 it is near-certain: the old check-12 probe
317	  missed on 500 of 500 runs against the real block. Use one of three forms instead. When the
318	  producer's status does not
319	  matter, use process substitution: `grep -qF -- "$lit" < <(printf '%s' "$block")`. When the
320	  status matters, capture the producer into a variable, check its status, then match the variable
321	  the same way; declare a `local` on its own line, and under `set -e` write the capture as the left
322	  side of `||`. In place of `head -1` or `grep -m1 … | sed`, use `sed -n 1p`; in place of
323	  `awk '…{print $2; exit}'`, take the first match in awk's `END` block. Do not use a here-string:
324	  Homebrew bash 5.3.15 deadlocks on one over about 512 bytes (see the LOCAL ONLY entry). Do not use
325	  `>/dev/null` in place of `-q`, and do not use a `sed` script with `q`. `ci/actionlint/run.sh`
326	  check 13 bans the pattern in every tracked `*.sh`, workflow, `moon.yml`, `.moon/**/*.yml` and
327	  `lefthook.yml`. The rule reads only the next command word after the pipe, so a reader inside a
328	  subshell or a brace group, a reader behind a wrapper word, and a `|&` pipe are not seen — see
329	  `ci/actionlint/README.md` L33–L41. Its allowlist, `EARLY_EXIT_READER_ALLOWED`, ships empty. Its
330	  fixtures live in `ci/actionlint/fixtures/early-exit/*.txt`, because check 13 also scans
331	  `run.sh`. Check 12 keeps
332	  a second opinion on each missing literal: a `literal-disagreement` row means `grep` and a bash
333	  `case` match disagree, which is evidence of a second mechanism. Keep that run's whole output for
334	  SMA-647 before you re-run.

342	## Fixture git repositories: no background maintenance (SMA-708)
343	
344	- A fixture repository under `ci/` in which any process runs `git commit`, `merge`, `fetch`,
345	  `pull`, `am`, `rebase` or `cherry-pick`, or which receives a push, sets
346	  `maintenance.auto false` and `gc.auto 0` with `git config` directly after `git init`. This
347	  includes git calls that an external tool (release-plz, semantic-release, PSR) makes in it.
348	- Why: after such a command, git starts a detached `git maintenance run --auto`. It writes
349	  `.git/objects/maintenance.lock` while the fixture's `shutil.rmtree` or `rm -rf` runs. On Python
350	  3.12 that raced into `FileNotFoundError: 'maintenance.lock'` (7 of 2,400 runs under load).
351	- A fixture with only `init`, `add`, `tag`, `ls-files` or `rm --cached` needs no keys. If you add
352	  one of the commands above to such a fixture, add the two keys in the same edit.
353	- Do not hide the race with `ignore_errors=True`, a retry, or `|| true`.
354	- Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-27-sma-708-git-maintenance-fixtures-design.md`.

356	## A nested `moon` call that targets a fixture workspace (SMA-714)
357	
358	- A gate that runs `moon` against a DIFFERENT workspace (a throwaway fixture) runs it with an
359	  allowlist environment: `env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH="$PATH" TMPDIR=… LANG=… PROTO_HOME=…
360	  PROTO_REPORTER=text MOON_WORKSPACE_ROOT="<fixture>"`. `ci/moon-diagnosis/run.sh` is the worked
361	  example.
362	- Why: moon passes its own `MOON_*` and `PROTO_*` variables to a task. An inherited
363	  `MOON_WORKSPACE_ROOT` moves the nested run to the real workspace (MEASURED: it failed with
364	  `app::missing_config` when the variable pointed to another directory). An inherited
365	  `PROTO_MOON_VERSION` overrides the fixture's `.prototools` pin, because proto reads
366	  `PROTO_<TOOL>_VERSION` first. One probe also printed `Base revision: N/A` under inherited `CI`
367	  and `GITHUB_*` variables. A second probe on 2026-09-28 with the same variable names did not
368	  show it, so that cause is not confirmed. `repo:moon-diagnosis-exec` asserts
369	  `Base revision: <sha>` on every run.
370	- Use an allowlist, not a denylist such as `unset MOON_*`. A new variable passes a denylist, and
371	  `env` output can hold multi-line values.
372	- This rule does NOT apply to a nested call that must target the REAL workspace, for example the
373	  nested `moon query` in `repo:affected-smoke`. That call needs the inherited environment.
374	- A fixture that commits also sets `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1` on every
375	  `git` call and local `commit.gpgsign false` and `tag.gpgsign false`. The development Mac signs
376	  every commit through 1Password, and a locked vault makes an unguarded fixture commit hang or fail.
